body_markdown:
The long-running infected blood scandal continues to raise serious concerns in the UK, with victims and campaigners calling on the Government to address problems within the compensation process.


Campaigners are urging Prime Minister Andy Burnham to take action over what they describe as unnecessary delays, complicated procedures and difficult evidence requirements affecting people seeking compensation. Their concerns come after the conclusion of the Infected Blood Inquiry, which examined one of the most serious treatment failures in the history of the National Health Service.


## What Was the Infected Blood Scandal?


The infected blood scandal involved thousands of people who contracted serious infections after receiving contaminated blood or blood products through NHS treatment.


Between the 1970s and early 1990s, more than 30,000 people in the UK are estimated to have been infected with HIV, hepatitis C or both after receiving contaminated blood products.


Many of those affected were people who needed blood transfusions or treatment for conditions such as haemophilia. Instead of receiving safe treatment, they were exposed to infections that could cause severe and lifelong health problems.


The consequences have been devastating for victims and their families. Thousands of people have died, while survivors have continued to experience serious health, financial and emotional difficulties.


The Infected Blood Inquiry spent years examining how the disaster happened, how authorities responded and why victims were not protected or adequately supported.


The inquiry's findings have increased pressure on the Government to ensure that compensation is delivered fairly and efficiently.


## Billions Allocated for Compensation


A compensation scheme for people affected by the infected blood scandal was announced in 2024.


The Government allocated approximately £11.8 billion for compensation, with the Infected Blood Compensation Authority, known as IBCA, responsible for administering payments.


The scheme is intended to provide financial recognition to people who suffered because of infected blood and blood products. It also aims to compensate eligible families and affected individuals for the wide-ranging consequences of the scandal.


However, campaigners argue that the process has not moved quickly enough.


Figures cited by IBCA show that thousands of people have now been asked to begin their claims. By late August, 3,512 people had received compensation, with total payments exceeding £2.25 billion.


While these payments represent significant progress, campaign groups say a large proportion of eligible victims are still waiting.


## Campaigners Raise Concerns Over Evidence Rules


One of the biggest concerns surrounding the compensation scheme involves the evidence that claimants may be expected to provide.


The Hepatitis C Trust has criticised what it considers to be excessively demanding evidence requirements in some cases.


For families dealing with events that happened decades ago, locating documents can be extremely difficult. Records may have been lost, destroyed or never created in the first place.


Campaigners have pointed to cases in which relatives have reportedly faced difficulties proving aspects of their relationship with people who died following infections linked to contaminated blood.


For grieving families, having to search for historic records can create another layer of distress.


The central concern is that people who have already suffered because of the scandal could face further emotional strain while attempting to demonstrate their eligibility for compensation.


## A Complicated System for Victims


Campaigners have also criticised the complexity of the compensation scheme.


The system covers a wide range of circumstances, meaning that calculating compensation can involve numerous factors. However, campaigners argue that the complexity can make the process difficult for ordinary people to understand.


Glenn Wilkinson, founder of the Contaminated Blood Campaign, has argued that victims expected a compensation process that would be straightforward and accessible.


According to campaigners, people with broadly similar experiences may sometimes receive different levels of compensation because of the way individual circumstances are assessed.


This has led to calls for the system to be reviewed and simplified wherever possible.


For victims, the issue is not simply about receiving money. Compensation is also seen as part of the wider process of recognising the harm caused and acknowledging the failures that allowed the scandal to happen.


## Why the Issue Remains Important


The end of the Infected Blood Inquiry does not mean that the consequences of the scandal have disappeared.


Many survivors continue to live with health complications, while families are still dealing with the loss of relatives.


The compensation process therefore represents an important part of the Government's response.


Campaigners want payments to reach eligible victims without unnecessary delays. They also want the system to recognise the practical difficulties involved in providing evidence about events that may have occurred 30, 40 or even 50 years ago.


The issue has particular significance because many victims have spent decades campaigning for recognition and justice.


For some families, compensation is arriving only after years of illness, financial hardship and bereavement.


## Government Says It Remains Committed


The Government has acknowledged that victims of the infected blood scandal suffered a profound injustice.


Officials have also said that the conclusion of the inquiry does not represent the end of the Government's responsibility towards the affected community.


IBCA has said it recognises that historic records can be difficult to locate and that evidence from decades ago may no longer be available.


The authority says claims are considered using a balance-of-probabilities approach. In simple terms, this means evidence can be accepted when it is considered more likely than not that an event occurred.


IBCA has also stated that its claim managers use a trauma-informed approach and can work with claimants to identify information from different sources.


These measures are intended to make the process more accessible to people who may not have conventional documentary evidence.


Nevertheless, campaigners believe further changes are necessary to ensure the compensation system delivers the fairness and simplicity victims were promised.


## What Happens Next?


Pressure is now building on the Government to respond to the concerns raised by campaign groups and affected families.


Campaigners have prepared letters and supporting material to present to Downing Street, calling for action on compensation delays and evidence requirements.


The issue is likely to remain an important test of the Government's commitment to the infected blood community.


The compensation scheme was created following years of campaigning and the extensive work of the Infected Blood Inquiry. Its success will ultimately be judged by whether eligible victims can access the support they are entitled to without facing unnecessary obstacles.


For survivors and bereaved families, the demand is straightforward: they want recognition, fair treatment and timely compensation after decades of suffering.


The infected blood scandal remains a painful chapter in NHS history. Although billions of pounds have been allocated and thousands of payments have been made, many affected people are still waiting.


As the compensation programme continues, campaigners will be watching closely to see whether the Government can simplify the process, resolve outstanding concerns and ensure that victims are not left waiting even longer for justice.


## Frequently Asked Questions


### What was the infected blood scandal?


The infected blood scandal involved people in the UK being given contaminated blood or blood products that resulted in infections including HIV and hepatitis C, particularly during the 1970s, 1980s and early 1990s.


### How many people were affected?


More than 30,000 people in the UK contracted HIV, hepatitis C or related infections after receiving contaminated blood or blood products. More than 3,000 deaths have been associated with the scandal.


### How much compensation has the Government allocated?


The Government announced approximately £11.8 billion for compensation for people affected by the infected blood scandal.


### Who administers the compensation scheme?


The Infected Blood Compensation Authority, or IBCA, is responsible for administering the compensation scheme.


### Why are campaigners calling for changes?


Campaigners have raised concerns about delays, complicated claim procedures and the level of evidence some applicants may be asked to provide, particularly when dealing with events that happened decades ago.


### Has the Infected Blood Inquiry finished?


The inquiry has concluded its work, but the Government's compensation and support commitments continue.


## Source


*The Independent* on 2 September 2026, alongside statements and figures attributed in that report to the Infected Blood Compensation Authority, the Hepatitis C Trust, campaigners and the UK Government.

Compensation eligibility, claim requirements and Government policies may change, so readers should consult official Government or IBCA information for the latest details.
